verdicts.evidence: The local import binds os to the operating system module, and the if condition directly compares os.name at f1:12-13 (s1).
The condition in s1 is equality against the literal nt, without negation, and s2 places the guarded code on its then side.
The condition reads os.name, an operating system property, so the os category fits (s1).

The branch has one condition, os.name equal to nt, in both the original and derived code (f1:13, f2:13). The regions s3 and s4 are its then bodies, so c1 alone satisfies the combination and the minimum is one.
The derived code places the download and execution inside the OS condition, with no alternative payload branch (f2:13-18). The test enables those operations rather than changing their target.
The then branch activates execution when os.name is nt; it does not test for analysis or sandbox tooling (f2:13-16).
The OS equality check restricts the download and execution to the nt platform, while ordinary installation continues after the condition (f2:13-18). This supports targeting as the gate's purpose.

The original guarded block is s3, and the corresponding derived block s4 remains inside the same OS equality then branch (f2:13-16). Both sink calls s5 and s6 occur directly inside s4, requiring no witness hops.

The sink calls occur only inside the guarded run method body (f2:11-16); calling the method through its install registration still encounters the OS test (f2:29-30). Neither supplied file contains a separate caller or entry into those sink expressions that bypasses the condition.

The requests import at f2:14 binds the network client used by the get call in s5. The response text is stripped of pre tags and passed directly to the built-in exec in s6, supporting download and execution of downloaded code.
